name: Formed natural-latex rubber objects
summary: By about 1700-1600 BCE people at El Manatí in Mexico were making solid balls of natural rubber from tree latex and placing them in offerings.
description: Latex was coagulated and shaped into freestanding natural-rubber objects. Some analyzed El Manatí balls have layered strips; the authors attribute their material to Castilla elastica, but these imaged objects are not securely matched to the earliest phase-A examples. The formulations and mechanical properties of individual ancient objects remain unresolved.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

impact.note: A new elastic material whose balls served many Mesoamerican societies for generations, with later rubber processing as its few successors.

date.label: Approximately 1700–1600 BCE
date.basis: The 2024 study attributes the earliest objects to the site’s phase A, approximately 1700–1600 BCE, using its published archaeological context; object-by-object dating remains limited.

events.statement: In approximately 1700–1600 BCE people placed some shaped rubber balls in the El Manatí offering deposits.
events.scope: Shaped natural-rubber balls in the early El Manatí offering contexts. Layered construction is documented on some site objects but not securely linked to the early examples.
events.population: People who deposited offerings at the El Manatí springs
events.caveats: Dates are archaeological phase attribution, not precise dates for every recovered ball. The site includes objects of later or unknown provenance; layer-imaged objects have not been identified with the phase-A examples. Offerings do not establish ballgame rules or play. Later experiments cannot establish the ancient mixture, species identification for each specimen, or mechanical performance; the 2024 analysis detected no plant additive and cannot rule one out.

evidence.locator: “Sacred ancient Olmec site: El Manatí” and “Conclusions”
evidence.supports: Some recovered rubber balls are attributed to phase A, approximately 1700–1600 BCE, in an offering context. Imaging identifies strips in some site objects, not demonstrably the same phase-A objects.
